column1: # Shared corpus of robots.txt questions (RFC 9309), kept byte for byte in the WebFlux and WebLookup tests.
# One row = one question: robots.txt body (\n and \r are escapes), the crawler name, the URL path (with query), and what RFC 9309 answers.
# `webflux` / `weblookup`: `=` means the implementation gives the RFC answer; `allow` or `disallow` is the answer it gives instead;
# `defect` means its answer is wrong today (the test pins what it answers now, so fixing it turns the row red until it is changed to `=`).
# A row that differs from the RFC carries a note: `choice:` (on purpose) or `defect:` (to fix).
# Change both copies together: scripts/check-shared-copies.ps1 in the umbrella fails when they differ.

column8: a pattern is a prefix, not a path segment
an empty value is the canonical allow-all file
order in the file does not matter
the star may cover a.php: the last piece sits at the end
the query is part of what is matched
only the most specific group applies; the * group is not merged in
an escaped reserved character is compared as written
the Bot group is real and empty, so Bot may fetch everything; it is not sent to the * group
a Sitemap line between two User-agent lines does not end the group
a character outside ASCII is compared as its escaped UTF-8 octets
an escaped unreserved character is decoded before the comparison
the hex digits of an escape are compared in one case
an escaped reserved character stays an escape, so it is not the wildcard
choice: WebLookup applies rules that precede any User-agent line to every agent (the safe direction); WebFlux drops them as the RFC grammar gives them no group
choice: WebFlux takes the product token from a full User-Agent string; WebLookup compares what the caller passes, so the caller passes the token
